text: The following question stood in the name of Dr Chia Shi-Lu – 1 To ask the Minister for Health in light of the recent incident concerning mistakes in computation for Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) subsidies (a) how often are audits conducted for individual clinics' CHAS-related accounts; (b) whether subsidy computations can be computed onsite so that patients can verify the amounts themselves; and (c) whether the Ministry will consider building inhouse computation capabilities so that this task need not be outsourced.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: This central system is owned by the Ministry of Health (MOH) and managed by our vendor NCS Pte Ltd.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: On 16 September 2018, the system was migrated to a new Government data centre, due to the Government’s planned decommissioning of the old data centre where the system was originally located.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: As a result, healthcare subsidy tiers of some individuals were computed without the corresponding full income information of these individuals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: The first run of the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) means tests after the system migration took place on 18 September.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: The first discrepancy in means-test results was identified by the CHAS processing team on 24 September, and NCS was immediately alerted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: The team then subsequently identified five more cases between 9 October and 2 November, and alerted NCS on each occasion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Three of the six cases were applications that required some manual verification from the CHAS processing team who detected the discrepancies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: The other three cases were appeals from CHAS applicants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Two were assessed to be legitimate appeals for higher subsidies and were approved.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Those who received lower subsidies will have the shortfall reimbursed, and their subsidies set to the correct levels going forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked about the checks and audits on the system and means-test results.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: To ensure the means-test status and healthcare subsidy levels are updated, a refresh of an individual’s data is automatically triggered every two years, or sooner should an individual request for an updated means-test or make an appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: We agree with Dr Chia Shi-Lu that it is useful to inform CHAS beneficiaries of their subsidies at each deduction so that they can also verify that their subsidy levels and balances are accurate and updated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: We plan to look into this during future rounds of system enhancements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: As for the means-test system, the regime of checks and audits are in line with overall Government Information Technology (IT) Policies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: These cover areas, including software development, test management, systems resiliency and cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Recent audits on the means-test system include one by GovTech on IT management process compliance from July to October 2018, and another initiated by MOH on cybersecurity in August 2018.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Where changes or enhancements are made to the system, MOH adheres to the quality assurance process stipulated for Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: This would include requirements on software component testing, end-to-end system integration testing, user acceptance testing, performance test, security test and production environment shakedown tests.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: For some systems, a set of transactions may also be performed at launch or migration to verify accuracy before going “live”.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Additional monitoring may be undertaken during the initial period of time after going “live”.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: The extent of testing in each case would depend on the assessed risk.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: The means-test system concerned is a mature system that has been running since 2012.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Based on the scope of this migration, the tests and validations were scoped and performed accordingly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Thereafter, the means-test system was migrated to the new data center.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Unfortunately, NCS deployed a wrong version of a software file to one of the servers in the new data centre.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: In other words, the scope of test and post-production validation was appropriate and in accordance with the project’s assessed risk, but the wrong version of the file was thereafter used, instead of the one that had been tested.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: And that applied to one of the servers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira also raised questions on outsourcing versus inhouse development.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: To deliver digital solutions and deploy IT systems effectively, the Government adopts a mix of IT development approaches, including outsourcing, co-sourcing and also in-sourcing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: If the solution is commercially mature, Government agencies are more likely to outsource, so as to better manage cost and leverage on the capacity, competency and also the scale available in the market.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Increasingly, the Government is also co-sourcing the development of critical systems with key vendors to ensure high systems quality and reliability, as well as interoperability across the Government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: In public healthcare, we take a similar approach.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: This allows us to move at a pace needed to support the volume of IT system requirements across the healthcare system, while ensuring that core capabilities continue to be developed internally.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: As we tap on technological solutions to raise productivity and improve the provision of healthcare services and support to Singaporeans, we are keenly aware that system vulnerabilities and risks exist and they do have to be carefully managed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Where IT systems are outsourced to vendors, we also have to closely supervise their work, monitor their performance and manage vendor risks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: We constantly seek to improve our quality assurance frameworks and review IT processes and outsourcing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong
text: Following this incident, MOH has started a review of our testing and deployment processes to identify areas that can be further strengthened.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first has to do with the scale of the error and the cost because the error did not just happen for CHAS but also affected outpatient subsidies, MediShield Life premium subsidies, subsidies for intermediate and long-term care and the disability assistance schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what is the scale of the error beyond CHAS and what is the cost?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second question is: if it affected these other subsidy schemes, too, does it mean that the means-testing data is so integrated that one error in one part would affect all the other parts with regard to a particular individual, for example, who is receiving subsidies across all these different schemes?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of the information that is affected, income information for a particular individual would remain similar.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, yes, if one aspect of the information is compromised, then it may affect the way in which that individual's subsidy tiers are calculated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The way in which we design the system is for convenience.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there is a similar backend to all of these subsidy tiers, and each time a request is being made, one goes back to the base information for that particular individual.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to that extent, yes, Assoc Prof Goh is right.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But ultimately, the integrity of the system depends on the various crosschecks and the verifications that are done before the information is then put out.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this case, there was one particular file that affected the base information, which is why when computing subsidy levels, the information was incomplete and, therefore, some subsidy levels were wrongly assigned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The first is that it appears from the timeline there was about a one-and-half months' lapse between discovery of the first discrepancy and the conclusion that it was a systemic error.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, is it the case that the vendor did not conclude there was a need to check for whether there was a systemic error upon being notified of the very first discrepancy?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The second question is: is it possible for the Ministry to clarify today the extent of recoverability of costs from the vendor?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And the last question is: will the decision to outsource this particular type of system, which is means-testing, will that be reviewed in light of this case?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The timeline I gave earlier takes into account the amount of time for the CHAS team to pick up the error, flag it to NCS and, within about three weeks or so, the error was fixed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What the vendor did not realise at that point in time was the fixing of that error meant that all cases moving forward would be correct, but it did not account for the fact that those that had been processed up to that point in time still had mismatched subsidy information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The error itself was fixed a few weeks later.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, from that time onwards, no other errors would occur.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Between that time and when this was then announced, steps were taken to identify the scope of the persons who were involved, how each of them was affected – whether up or down – and the extent to which remediation would take place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And once that was determined, this was announced back in February, earlier this month.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the last question by Assoc Prof Theseira, this system still remains the most convenient because it allows there to be one avenue where the information is contained and one source at which all of these would be determined when an applicant comes and makes an application for subsidy, whether it is CHAS, long-term care or for some other subsidy schemes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the best way in which this can be fixed and to ensure that this problem does not arise again, is to really strengthen and make more resilient the way in which testing is done, either at the time migration takes place or at some stage thereafter, to continue to monitor even after it goes "live", as I had mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Fixing the problem at its root requires these levels of resiliency to be improved, not so much to change the system architecture altogether.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Order of the Day.
